summary: Defines Management Information Base objects for monitoring batteries in managed devices, so network management software can read battery status through SNMP.

eli5.summary: A fuel gauge for gadgets that a network manager can read remotely.

questions: how to monitor battery with snmp
what is a battery charging cycle
subtitle: SNMP objects that let a management system watch a device's batteries: charge, age, state and alarms.

tldr.problem: More and more managed devices run on batteries, but network management systems had no standard way to read battery status or be warned that a battery needed replacing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7577 defines the BATTERY-MIB module: one table with a row per battery, holding static properties, live state and alarm thresholds, plus seven notifications.
tldr.outcome: A management system can read charge, capacity, charging cycles and temperature over SNMP, ask for a charging state change, and be notified of low, critical or aging batteries.

facts.label: Table rows
facts.value: One per battery, indexed by entPhysicalIndex

today: RFC 7577 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2015. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Monitor Batteries
sections.content:
Many managed devices, such as notebook computers, netbooks and smartphones, contain batteries that supply power when they are disconnected from the electrical grid. Locally, charging is normally handled by automatic functions on the device and by its user. RFC 7577 adds a way for network management systems to monitor those batteries through a Management Information Base (MIB) module, read with SNMP.

The module meets the battery monitoring requirements of RFC 6988. It is an Energy Managed Object in the framework of RFC 7326, and it adds battery-specific information on top of the more generic energy monitoring of RFC 7460. It covers the current charge, the age (charging cycles), the state (for example, being recharged), the last usage and the maximum energy a battery can provide.

Devices often already measure these values for local control, so for many devices only extra software is needed. The older UPS MIB in RFC 1628 covers batteries inside uninterruptible power supplies, but its information is limited and tailored to UPS needs. Very small backup batteries, such as the one that keeps a PC clock running, are not explicitly in scope.
sections.eli5: Phones and laptops already know how full their batteries are. This document gives a standard way for a faraway computer to ask them and get an answer.

sections.title: A Generic Battery Model
sections.content:
The module uses a generic abstraction of batteries that does not depend on a particular battery technology. The technology is only identified by a number. Methods for charging, which vary greatly between technologies, are not modeled individually.

Instead there is one simple charging model with four states: charging, maintaining charge, not charging and discharging. Control is limited to requests to move between these states. A charging controller with more internal states has to map them onto these four. For finer control, the RFC says other MIB modules would have to be developed.

The module is an interface between the management system and the battery charging controller. External batteries can be supported as long as their charging controller is connected to the SNMP applications that implement the module. The interface between the controller and the batteries themselves is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Every battery type is described with the same few words: filling up, topping off, resting, or emptying. Fancier details are left to other documents.

sections.title: The Battery Table
sections.content:
All status objects live in one table, batteryTable, with one conceptual row per battery. Rows are indexed by entPhysicalIndex from the Entity MIB (RFC 6933), and a compliant implementation needs an Entity MIB implementation that meets entity4CRCompliance. If a battery is replaced and the new one uses the same physical connector, it MUST get the same entPhysicalIndex. Batteries SHOULD have entPhysicalClass set to battery(14).

The table has three groups of objects:

  • Static properties (OIDs ending 1 to 9): identifier, firmware version, type, technology, design voltage, number of cells, design capacity, maximum charging current and trickle charging current.
  • Current state (OIDs ending 10 to 18): actual capacity, charging cycle count, time of the last cycle, operational and administrative charging state, actual charge, voltage, current and temperature.
  • Notification support (OIDs ending 19 to 25): six alarm thresholds and a cell identifier.

Units are explicit: voltage in millivolts, capacity and charge in milliampere hours, current in milliamperes and temperature in deci-degrees Celsius. Many objects use special values to say a measurement is unknown, such as ffffffff hex for actual capacity, charge, voltage and cycle count, and 7fffffff hex for actual current and temperature.
sections.eli5: There is one big sheet with a row for each battery. Some columns never change, like its size. Others change all the time, like how full it is. The last few hold the warning levels.

sections.title: Identity, Technology and Charging Cycles
sections.content:
The batteryType object tells primary (not rechargeable) batteries from rechargeable (secondary) ones and from capacitors. batteryTechnology is a number from an IANA registry, not a fixed list, because technologies change quickly. Initial values include 3 for zinc-carbon, 11 for alkaline, 12 for lead-acid, 18 for lithium-ion, 19 for lithium polymer and 20 for double layer capacitor; 1 means unknown and 2 means other. New entries are added by Expert Review, and only for technologies in commercial use and relevant to standardized battery monitoring.

Two identifiers are involved. batteryIdentifier mirrors the identifier set by the manufacturer and follows the battery, so a management system can trace it when it is moved to another device. entPhysicalUUID from the Entity MIB identifies the slot and stays the same when the battery in that slot is replaced.

A charging cycle follows the Smart Battery definition: discharging by a total equal to the design capacity of the battery. A cycle may contain several partial charges and discharges, and the next one starts immediately after one completes. For primary batteries the cycle count is always 0.
sections.eli5: A battery has its own name tag that goes with it, while the slot has a separate label that stays put. A full cycle means you have used up as much power as the battery can hold in total, even if you did it in small sips.

sections.title: Charge Control and Notifications
sections.content:
batteryChargingOperState is read-only and reports the real state: unknown(1), charging(2), maintainingCharge(3), noCharging(4) or discharging(5). To request a change, a manager writes batteryChargingAdminState: notSet(1) (the default, where the controller uses its own policies), charge(2), doNotCharge(3) or discharge(4).

A write is only a request. The controller may refuse it or even choose another state, for example it may enter discharging(5) at any time if the battery is needed to supply power. The admin state does not change automatically when the operational state changes, but the controller SHOULD move to the requested state as soon as conditions allow. A manager that wants to react to a change can poll the operational state or use the charging state notification.

Seven notifications are defined: charging state change not caused by a write to the admin state, low battery, critical battery, aging, temperature, battery connected and battery disconnected. Notifications 2 to 5 can name a specific cell through batteryCellIdentifier. Several have rate rules; for example, the temperature notification should not be repeated for the same battery or cell within 10 minutes, except right after the monitoring system is reinitialized. Low and critical notifications should not be sent while the battery is charging.
sections.eli5: You can ask the battery to charge, rest or drain, but it is allowed to say no if it needs to keep your gadget running. It also rings different bells for low, very low, old, hot, plugged in and unplugged.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Several read-write objects are sensitive. An attacker who can set batteryChargingAdminState could drain batteries and switch off devices that run only on battery, and if the low charge and voltage alarm thresholds can also be set, the attack goes unnoticed. Setting an alarm threshold to its off value (0, or 7fffffff hex for temperature) silences the alarm, which may lead to data loss, damaged batteries or devices, or replacement of a battery that was still good.

Read access has its own risks. The number, types, firmware versions and ageing of batteries might be trade secrets. For battery-powered devices that can be tied to a person, charging cycles, charge level and temperature can reveal habits, so monitoring should occur only with proper authorization.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features, and implementations claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy with the User-based Security Model and AES. Deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Anyone who could change the settings might drain a battery or turn off the warning bell. So only trusted people should be allowed to read or change them, using the secure version of SNMP.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: The charging state cannot be determined.

items.label: charging
items.desc: The charge of the battery increases.

items.label: noCharging
items.desc: No current flows between the battery and outside circuits.

items.label: discharging
items.desc: The battery supplies power or is drained on purpose; its charge decreases.
